What is Ansible Automation Platform

In one sentence: AAP is Red Hat's enterprise product for running Ansible automation as a shared, controlled service — with a web console, access control, an audit trail and support — instead of every engineer running playbooks from their own laptop.

Why teams move from plain Ansible to the platform:

  • One place to run automation — jobs run on servers, not laptops, with logs kept.
  • Control — who may run what, on which machines, with which credentials.
  • Self-service — non-experts launch approved automation from a simple form.
  • Secrets stay safe — credentials are stored encrypted and used without being shown.
  • Evidence — every job records who ran it, when, where and what happened.
Every request enters through the gateway; the controller pushes work out to execution nodes, which touch the managed machines.

Each component, described

ComponentWhat it doesPlain-words analogy
Platform GatewayThe single web entry point. One address, one login for all services below. Holds the user database and enforces unified RBAC on every request.The reception desk and badge system
Automation ControllerThe engine. Stores projects (playbook repos), inventories (machine lists), credentials and job templates; schedules and tracks every job.The operations control room
Execution nodesThe worker machines where jobs actually execute, connected to the controller by the receptor mesh. Grouped into Instance Groups so work can be pinned to specific machines.The workshop floor
Execution Environment (EE)A container image holding Ansible plus all needed collections and libraries. Every job runs inside one, so runs are identical everywhere.A sealed toolbox, same tools every time
Automation HubThe private content library: certified Ansible collections and EE container images, served locally.The parts warehouse
Event-Driven Ansible (EDA)Watches event sources (monitoring alerts, webhooks, queues) and reacts by launching automation according to rulebooks.A smoke detector wired to the sprinklers
PostgreSQLOne database service; each component keeps its own data in it.The filing cabinet
RedisCache and internal message broker between gateway services.The pneumatic message tubes

How RBAC works in AAP

RBAC = role-based access control. AAP builds it from four blocks:

BlockPlain meaningQuestion it answers
OrganizationA walled garden. Every resource lives in exactly one org, and you only see the orgs you belong to.What can you SEE?
Team and UserThe people in the garden. Object permissions are granted to teams, people join teams.Who are you?
RoleThe verbs. Organization Admin = manage everything inside; Organization Member = view, plus whatever the team was granted (run this template, use this credential).What can you DO?
Instance GroupThe machines an org's jobs may run on.WHERE do your jobs run?
RBAC concept Memorize one line: Organization decides what you SEE, Role decides what you DO, Instance Group decides WHERE your jobs run.

How the layers fit together — one organization, top to bottom:

The layers and how they relate: the org owns everything; the team's users run the job template; the job template combines the project, inventory and credential, and runs on the org's instance group.

Every request — from the web console or the raw API — passes the same check:

How the platform decides every single request.

Key properties, each proven live later in this guide:

  • Deny by default. A new user can do nothing until an org, team and role are granted.
  • Invisible, not just locked. Another org's resources are not listed at all; a direct request by ID gets 403.
  • Enforced at the API. Greyed-out buttons are a courtesy; the real gate answers 201 or 403. Scripts and CLI hit the same wall.
  • Least privilege with built-in roles. A safe operator profile (run but not change) needs no custom role engineering.

Architecture: single-node AAP on RHEL

The smallest real deployment: every component on one RHEL virtual machine, installed with the containerized installer (the recommended installer for RHEL; the old RPM installer was removed in AAP 2.7).

Single-node topology: the whole platform on one RHEL VM. This is exactly what scenario B deploys for team-b.
  • Node count: 1 RHEL VM (4 vCPU / 16 GB RAM / 60 GB disk minimum).
  • Jobs run on the same VM (it is a hybrid node), or on execution nodes you add later.
  • Grows sideways: the same installer can later add execution nodes — that is exactly what the scenario A platform did (one control VM plus two execution VMs).
  • No high availability: one VM down = platform down. Jobs that already ran are safe (database on the VM), but nothing new runs until it is back.
  • Storage: local disk only — a single node needs no shared storage.
  • Best for: pilots, labs, small teams, edge sites — and scenario B in this guide.

Architecture: full HA AAP on RHEL

For production where automation is business-critical, every layer gets at least two nodes and the database moves to an external, customer-managed cluster:

Enterprise HA topology on RHEL: redundant gateway, controller, hub and EDA layers behind a load balancer, with an external database.
  • Gateway x2 behind a load balancer — login and API stay up if one fails.
  • Controller x2 — control-plane redundancy; a failed node's jobs are picked up.
  • Hub x2 — content and EE images stay available. This is the one layer with a shared storage requirement: both hub nodes must see the same content directory (see the list below).
  • EDA x2 — event listeners keep listening.
  • Execution nodes, 2 or more — this is also the scaling layer: add nodes per team, per datacenter or per security zone, and group them with Instance Groups.
  • External PostgreSQL + external Redis — the platform's state survives any platform node.
  • Typical minimum: about 10 RHEL VMs plus the database cluster. All still installed and upgraded by the same containerized installer, from one inventory file.

Shared storage requirements at a glance

LayerNeeds shared storage?Supported options (examples)
Automation Hub, 2+ nodesyes — requiredNFS shared filesystem mounted by every hub node; or switch the hub backend to object storage: Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage
Gateway / Controller / EDA nodesnolocal disk on each node is enough
Execution nodesnolocal disk; jobs are sent to them over the receptor mesh
Database layernot storage — a serviceexternal PostgreSQL cluster (plus external Redis for a full-HA gateway)
Good to know The single-node and HA pictures are the SAME product and installer — the difference is only how many hosts appear in the installer inventory. You can start small and grow.

Architecture: AAP on OpenShift

If the customer already runs OpenShift, AAP can be installed as an operator from OperatorHub instead of on RHEL VMs:

AAP on OpenShift: the operator runs the platform as pods; jobs run as on-demand pods in container groups.
  • The operator installs and upgrades the platform and restarts anything that fails.
  • Availability from Kubernetes: pods reschedule automatically; no load balancer to build.
  • Jobs run as pods ("container groups"): each job gets a fresh pod, capacity comes from the cluster, and it scales to zero when idle.
  • Storage comes from the cluster as a StorageClass. The shared-storage requirement here is the hub's content volume, which must be RWX (ReadWriteMany — many pods, same volume). Examples: OpenShift Data Foundation / CephFS, an NFS storage class, AWS EFS, Azure Files. The database needs only a normal RWO block volume.
  • The self-service portal (a newer AAP add-on giving business users a catalog-style front door) ships as a Helm chart for OpenShift only — on RHEL-based AAP the native equivalent is job-template Surveys, which scenario A demonstrates live.
  • Trade-off: you must already have (and know how to run) an OpenShift cluster. VM-based execution nodes can still be attached for jobs that must run close to specific networks.

Scenario A: two teams share one AAP

The situation: two teams with totally separate work. They share nothing except the platform itself — one AAP, one subscription — and one shared inventory of RHEL machines that both teams automate. Requirement: neither team may see, run, or change the other team's automation.

The design, all applied as code (playbooks/rbac.yml):

  • One organization per team (tenant-a, tenant-b) — the SEE boundary.
  • One team + two users per org — an admin (Organization Admin) and an operator (Organization Member).
  • One dedicated execution node per team, bound via an instance group — the WHERE guarantee.
  • Own project, inventory, credentials, job template per team — even the git repos are separate private repos, each reached with the owning team's token only.
  • One shared inventory, owned by platform-admin. Both teams run against it; team-a additionally maintains it (fleet owner — may edit and add machines), team-b is use-only.
The deployed scenario A lab: one shared platform, one dedicated execution node per team.
Validated live This exact environment is running on the vSphere lab: AAP 2.7 (the newest release) containerized on RHEL 9. Everything below is from it.

Step 7 — the mirror world

The shared inventory, validated

The teams share one thing on purpose: the fleet of RHEL machines they automate. It is modeled once and shared safely — with delegated fleet ownership:

  • The inventory shared-rhel-fleet is owned by the platform-admin org.
  • team-a is the fleet owner: its team also holds Inventory Admin on this one object, so team-a may edit the inventory and add or remove machines. This shows how a single object-level role grant delegates real responsibility without making anyone a platform admin.
  • team-b is a consumer: granted Inventory Use only — it can run jobs against the fleet but any change attempt is refused (403).
  • Each team reaches the fleet with its own machine credential in its own org. (A platform rule found during validation: a credential cannot be granted to a team in another organization — so credentials stay per-org by design.)
  • Each team's fleet job still runs on that team's own execution node.
The shared-inventory pattern with delegated ownership: one fleet, two isolated teams — the owner team maintains the machine list, the consumer team only runs against it.
Validated live Both teams ran shared_report.yml against the shared fleet: each job reached both machines over SSH and each ran on the launching team's own execution node. team-a edited the inventory (HTTP 200) and added a test host (HTTP 201, removed again afterwards); team-b's edit attempt returned 403 Forbidden. Full results: docs/validation-results.md, raw evidence in evidence/.
Check (per team, as that team's admin)tenant-a (fleet owner)tenant-b (consumer)
Sees only its own job templatesyesyes
Other team's template by direct API request403403
Own job ran on own dedicated nodeyes (.31)yes (.32)
Can see and use the shared inventoryyesyes
Can edit the shared inventoryyes — 200no — 403
Can add a machine to the fleetyes — 201 (test host, cleaned up)not granted
Shared-fleet job reached both machinesyesyes
Shared-fleet job ran on own nodeyes (.31)yes (.32)
RBAC concept Roles are granted per OBJECT, not only per organization. Handing team-a the Inventory Admin role on one inventory delegates fleet maintenance to that team — while every other wall (templates, credentials, execution nodes, team-b's use-only limit) stays exactly as before.

Scenario B: each team gets its own AAP

The situation: the same two teams — but now the isolation requirement is absolute: no shared platform at all. Team B gets its own single-node AAP, designed and deployed for this guide.

What was deployed (with the same code pipeline as scenario A):

  • A new RHEL 9 VM aap-b (172.16.28.33, 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 60 GB) on the same vSphere lab.
  • AAP 2.7 containerized, true single node: gateway, controller, hub, EDA, database and job execution all on the one VM — the single-node architecture from the concepts section, made real.
  • Team B modeled on it as code: org team-b, team, admin + operator users, project, inventory, credential, job template — same model, new platform.
  • Git stays external: the project pulls team-b's existing private repo from the lab git server.
Scenario B: two completely separate platforms. The only thing they have in common is the network.

What "own platform" means in practice:

  • Own user database: accounts from one platform simply do not exist on the other.
  • Own RBAC, own admin: team-b runs its platform without any shared admin domain.
  • Own failure and upgrade domain: one platform down or upgrading does not touch the other.
  • Own database, certificates, backups, subscription allocation.

Scenario B, validated

The same test style as scenario A — log in as the users and prove it (playbooks/validate_b.yml):

CheckResult
team-b-admin logs into aap-b.redhat.local and sees only team-b automationpass
team-b job launches and succeedspass
The job executed on aap-b itself (single node = local execution)pass
tenant-a-admin's working platform-1 login against platform-2's API401 Unauthorized
team-b-admin's working platform-2 login against platform-1's API401 Unauthorized
Why 401 and not 403 On the shared platform a cross-tenant attempt returns 403 Forbidden — the platform knows who you are but refuses. Across two separate platforms it returns 401 Unauthorized — the other platform has never heard of you. That is the difference between logical and physical isolation, visible in one HTTP status.

Single node (RHEL)Enterprise HA (RHEL)On OpenShift
RHEL VMs needed1about 10 + external DB0 (needs an OCP cluster)
Survives a node failurenoyesyes (pods reschedule)
Execution capacitythe node itself (+ add nodes later)dedicated execution nodes, scale per team/siteon-demand job pods

Second choice: one shared platform or one per team

Scenario A — one shared AAPScenario B — own AAP per team
Isolation typeLogical (RBAC walls, proven with 403s)Physical (separate everything, proven with 401s)
Infrastructure1 platform (here: 3 VMs total for 2 teams)1 platform per team (here: +1 VM for a single-node)
Subscription useone pool, fully utilizedsplit per platform; often more total cost
Operationspatch, back up, upgrade ONE platformN platforms to patch, back up, upgrade
Shared fleet inventorynatural (validated here)not possible across platforms — each models the fleet separately
Blast radiusplatform outage affects all teamsoutage affects one team only
Upgrade freedomone version and one window for everyoneeach team upgrades when it wants
Team admin autonomyorg-admin inside the shared platformfull platform admin
Noise between teamsexecution isolated by dedicated nodes; control plane still sharednone
Best whenteams belong to one company, cost and central operations matter, isolation "cannot see or affect each other" is enoughhard compliance/regulatory separation, different companies, wildly different change cadences, or a team must own its platform end to end
Recommendation Rule of thumb: start with scenario A — RBAC isolation held up under live attack-style tests here. Move a team to scenario B only when a rule (not a feeling) demands physical separation. The as-code setup makes that move cheap: the same playbooks deployed both.

Reproduce everything

Nothing in this guide was clicked together. The whole environment — both platforms — comes from playbooks in this repository:

How everything in this guide was built and proven, end to end, as code.
  • Scenario A platform: provision.yml, prepare.yml, install_aap.yml, gitea.yml, rbac.yml, validate.yml.
  • Scenario B platform: same pipeline with install_aap_b.yml and rbac.yml -e rbac_model=rbac_b, then validate_b.yml.
  • Idempotent: re-running any of them changes nothing unless something drifted.
  • Secrets never enter the repo: they live in a gitignored secrets/ directory.
  • Teardown: teardown.yml removes the VMs cleanly.
AAP 2.7 (newest release, containerized) on RHEL 9, VMware vSphere. Scenario A: one all-in-one node + one dedicated execution node per tenant. Scenario B: one additional true single-node platform. RBAC defined as code with ansible.platform / ansible.controller. All checks in this guide were executed against the live environments; evidence in the repo.
